title: Choosing where state lives
objectives: Choose the smallest home for state: lift to a common parent first, and use the URL for shareable state
Spot fetched data that belongs in a useQuery cache, not in useState or a client store
Predict that every Context consumer re-renders on a new value, and explain how store selectors avoid it
Fix a provider's fresh value object with useMemo and useCallback so unrelated updates skip consumers

sources.title: React docs: Sharing State Between Components
React docs: Choosing the State Structure

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in a server-state library (TanStack Query) rather than a global client store like Zustand or Redux?

options.text: The list of users fetched from your /api/users endpoint
The text a user is typing into a form

questions.explanation: Server data is a cache of someone else's data: it needs fetching, deduping, caching, staleness, retries and invalidation — exactly what a server-state library provides. Theme, sidebar, and a form draft are genuine client state. Putting the users list in a client store means hand-rolling all the caching/invalidation a Query gives you for free.

questions.prompt: You store a rapidly-changing value (say, the current playback time) in a Context that wraps half the app. What happens on each tick?

options.text: Only components that read that specific field re-render
Every component consuming that context re-renders — even ones reading other fields
Nothing re-renders; React batches context updates away
React automatically memoizes the provider so consumers are skipped

questions.explanation: Context has no per-field subscription. When the provider's value changes identity, EVERY consumer re-renders regardless of which field it reads — and memo() on a consumer doesn't help. Nor does memoization of any kind, by hand or by React Compiler: the value genuinely changes on every tick, and React doesn't batch context updates away. High-frequency values want a ref, a store with selectors, or a split context. This is the cost that pushes people off Context for hot values.

questions.prompt: Two components three levels apart need to share one piece of state. What's the first thing to reach for?

options.text: Lift the state to their nearest common ancestor and pass it down
Add a global store so both can import it
Wrap the app in a Context immediately

questions.explanation: Colocation first: lift to the nearest common ancestor. Reach for Context or a store only when lifting causes real prop-drilling pain across many layers or many consumers. Globalizing by reflex is how everything ends up entangled in one store. The URL is the right owner only when a link should reproduce the state (a filter, a tab, a page number); nothing here says it should, and the URL is a place to share navigation state, not a shortcut around passing props.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical reason to choose a client store like Zustand over Context for frequently-changing, app-wide client state?

options.text: Components can subscribe to a slice, so unrelated updates don't re-render them
Zustand state survives a page refresh without extra code
Context values can't be persisted to localStorage

questions.explanation: Zustand's selector subscriptions re-render a component only when its selected slice changes; Context re-renders every consumer on any value change. The others are wrong: a Zustand store lives in memory just like a Context value, so surviving a refresh takes the `persist` middleware (or your own storage code) either way; neither tool is tied to TypeScript; and state that Context carries can be persisted just fine — persistence is a storage concern, not a transport one.

prompts.prompt: Remote data belongs in a server-state cache, not useState. Complete the TanStack Query call.
prompts.explanation: useQuery owns the fetch/cache/staleness/invalidation lifecycle for remote data. If you find yourself writing a useEffect that fetches and stores into useState, you're re-implementing a worse version of this.

prompts.prompt: Stop this provider from re-rendering every consumer on each render by giving the value a stable identity.
prompts.explanation: An inline object literal is a new identity every render, so every consumer re-renders. useMemo pins the identity to its deps, so consumers re-render only when user or logout actually changes. Stabilize the functions with useCallback too.

prompts.prompt: A search filter should be shareable via a link and survive a refresh, so it belongs in the URL. Read it in a Next.js App Router client component.
prompts.explanation: In the Next.js App Router, `useSearchParams()` from `next/navigation` (client components only) returns a read-only `URLSearchParams`; you change the query by navigating — `router.push`, or a `<Link>` to the new URL. Filters, tabs and pagination in the URL are linkable, bookmarkable and survive a reload — things component state can't give you. Reading `window.location.search` during render instead breaks server rendering (there is no `window` on the server) and doesn't re-render when a client-side navigation changes the query.

snippets.question: CountLabel reads only `count`. If you call setName("Bob") (count unchanged), does CountLabel re-render?
snippets.explanation: setName re-renders Provider, which builds a brand-new value object. Context compares by identity, so every consumer re-renders — including CountLabel, which never reads name. Context has no field-level subscription. To avoid this you split the context or use a store with selectors.
